articles.title: Approve Rosebank immediately
articles.proposal: Approve the Rosebank North Sea oil and gas project immediately.
articles.counter: Rosebank could support jobs and production, but immediate approval offers no guaranteed household price cut and must address the consenting evidence.
articles.critique: Rosebank could sustain offshore employment, engineering contracts and tax receipts, so its economic benefits deserve examination. But approving a field is different from delivering cheaper fuel. Its output would be predominantly oil, while the household heating problem is largely about gas. International trading also means domestic extraction does not automatically create a discounted British price. An immediate political commitment risks prejudging the environmental assessment rather than resolving it. The Commons Library records that the earlier consent was effectively quashed in January 2025 and fresh applications followed in July 2026. A ministerial answer on 14 September 2026 said the regulatory process was continuing; that dated answer does not establish the project's final status today. A credible approval case should therefore publish the assessment, realistic production timetable, public revenue implications and conditions protecting the environment. Workers and supply chains need a durable decision that survives scrutiny, alongside investment beyond the lifetime of one field.

articles.title: Restart licensing for new oil and gas fields
articles.proposal: Resume issuing exploration licences for new oil and gas fields.
articles.counter: New licences can encourage exploration, but they cannot guarantee discoveries, rapid production or insulation from international fuel prices.
articles.critique: A predictable licensing regime can support exploration businesses and preserve specialist skills. There is a legitimate debate about how much of Britain's continuing fuel demand should be supplied domestically. However, a licence is only an early step: commercially viable discoveries, finance, infrastructure and development consent must follow before production. That makes licensing a weak answer to an immediate cost of living crisis. The North Sea is also a mature basin, so ministers should distinguish slowing decline from reversing it. The Commons Library's September 2026 briefing describes the government's policy against new licences while allowing existing licensed projects to seek consent. Restarting rounds would therefore need a clear account of what additional investment is genuinely caused by the change. The trade-off is between possible future jobs and receipts, environmental impacts and capital committed to long-lived assets. Judging projects against realistic demand and price scenarios would be more informative than counting licences as energy delivered.

articles.title: Legalise onshore exploration in new licences
articles.proposal: Allow onshore oil and gas exploration through new licences.
articles.counter: Licensing onshore exploration does not settle local planning, environmental permissions or the separate restrictions on shale fracking.
articles.critique: Domestic onshore exploration could create some local contracts and identify useful resources. The proposal nevertheless needs much more precision about geography and drilling methods. Conventional exploration and high-volume hydraulic fracturing are different activities, and issuing a licence would not by itself resolve the permissions needed to drill or produce. A ministerial answer on 16 October 2026 confirmed that the effective shale-fracking moratorium continued for existing licences and distinguished conventional low-volume techniques. The same answer described forthcoming legislation, rather than establishing an already operative blanket statutory ban. Nearby residents would need clear protections for water, traffic, noise and site restoration, together with a meaningful planning process. Commercial success is uncertain, so promises of large tax receipts or cheap gas should not be booked in advance. Any assessment should compare the expected recoverable resource and development time with the disruption borne by host communities, rather than assuming permission to explore guarantees a productive industry.

articles.title: Abolish the Energy Profits Levy immediately
articles.proposal: Immediately remove the additional tax on oil and gas profits known as the Energy Profits Levy.
articles.counter: Removing the levy could improve investment incentives, but gives up public revenue without requiring firms to invest or cut British energy prices.
articles.critique: Frequent tax changes can discourage investment, and removing an additional profit tax could make some marginal developments more attractive. That is a real potential benefit for offshore workers and suppliers. The fiscal question is how much extra activity the tax cut would generate compared with the revenue lost on production that would happen anyway. A Treasury answer in July 2026 put the levy at 38%, alongside a 40% permanent regime, with reliefs affecting actual liabilities. Abolition therefore benefits existing profitable operations as well as possible new investment. Nothing in this measure requires recipients to spend the saving in Britain or sell fuel below market prices. HMRC has also published proposals for a different, price-triggered replacement after the levy ends; that proposal should not be confused with an existing additional charge. A credible costing needs investment responses, timing and the alternative use of lost revenue, rather than treating a producer tax cut as an automatic consumer saving.

articles.title: Change the North Sea regulator's objective and name
articles.proposal: Restore maximum economic extraction as the regulator's statutory objective, remove its Net Zero obligation and rename the North Sea Transition Authority the Oil & Gas Authority.
articles.counter: A new name and narrower objective cannot remove depletion or commercial constraints, while dropping emissions duties weakens accountability for production impacts.
articles.critique: A clearer regulatory mandate could help operators understand how investment proposals will be judged. But the premise needs care: the regulator's published strategy already combines maximising economic recovery with a duty to assist the net zero target. Economic recovery has therefore not simply disappeared from its framework. Removing the emissions element would change how competing costs and benefits are weighed, rather than uncovering resources by administrative instruction. The measure also needs to explain how the regulator would treat methane leaks, platform energy use and investment that reduces operational emissions. These affect the public interest even where oil and gas remain necessary. A focus on extraction could favour continued production, but cannot make every discovery commercially viable or replace depleted reservoirs. Parliament should assess the proposed statutory wording, the treatment of emissions and the consequences for taxpayers and offshore workers. Renaming the organisation provides little evidence of additional output or lower bills on its own.

articles.title: Abolish the Emissions Trading Scheme
articles.proposal: Abolish the UK Emissions Trading Scheme.
articles.counter: Scrapping carbon trading may reduce some firms' immediate costs, but removes a declining emissions cap and changes incentives for industrial investment.
articles.critique: Carbon costs can put pressure on energy-intensive businesses, especially when overseas competitors face weaker rules. Removing allowance purchases could therefore relieve some immediate costs, although the benefit would differ between firms. The UK scheme already provides free allocations to eligible installations to reduce the risk of production moving abroad. It also limits total covered emissions through a cap that falls over time. Abolition would remove both a compliance cost and that investment signal. A business that has already paid for cleaner equipment could find its competitive position weakened relative to a higher-emitting rival. Any claim about household savings needs to show how lower costs pass through wholesale markets and retail contracts, and what replaces the public revenue. The policy also interacts directly with border carbon adjustments: ending both instruments changes the whole competitive framework. A serious alternative should specify how emissions will be reduced, how exposed manufacturers will be supported and who bears the transition costs.

articles.title: Stop implementing the Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism
articles.proposal: Stop implementing the UK Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism, including the proposed charge affecting fertiliser imports.
articles.counter: Cancelling the border charge could help importers and farmers, but also removes protection for British producers paying domestic carbon costs.
articles.critique: Farmers and manufacturers using imported inputs have a legitimate interest in avoiding additional costs and complicated emissions paperwork. Cancelling the planned border charge would remove that prospective burden. However, the mechanism is intended to address a real competitive problem: British producers can pay a carbon price while equivalent imports escape it. HMRC's September 2026 policy paper says the charge is due to begin on 1 January 2027 and includes specified fertiliser imports, alongside several other industrial sectors. Its rates are intended to reflect domestic carbon costs after relevant reliefs, so the headline existence of a charge does not establish a uniform price rise. Abolishing it alone could disadvantage cleaner UK production; abolishing the domestic trading scheme as well would remove that particular imbalance but also the emissions incentive. The plan needs an integrated assessment of farmers, domestic fertiliser manufacturers, import competition and food prices, including how suppliers would pass any savings to customers.

articles.title: Repudiate AR7 contracts and scrap AR8
articles.proposal: Repudiate contracts for difference from allocation round 7 and cancel allocation round 8.
articles.counter: Repudiating awarded support risks legal costs and investor confidence, while removing contracts that can also return money when wholesale prices rise.
articles.critique: It is reasonable to scrutinise renewable support prices and the wider costs of connecting and balancing new generation. But rejecting existing contracts is a different decision from designing a better future auction. The government published round 7 results in January 2026, followed by round 7a results in February; those results describe contract offers, so the legal position must be checked project by project. Contracts for difference support a negotiated revenue level: generators receive top-ups when the reference price is lower, and pay back the difference when it is higher. Treating them as an unconditional subsidy misses that protection. Repudiation could trigger disputes or compensation claims, depending on the executed contracts and legislation. It could also increase the return investors demand for future British infrastructure if government commitments look unreliable. Cancelling round 8 may avoid future commitments, but requires a replacement plan for capacity, finance and energy security. Any claimed saving should deduct legal exposure and replacement supply costs.

articles.title: Implement the Fingleton Review immediately
articles.proposal: Implement the Fingleton Review's nuclear energy recommendations in full immediately.
articles.counter: Reducing unnecessary nuclear delays is useful, but implementation needs legislation, regulatory capacity and a deliverable construction and financing programme.
articles.critique: The Fingleton review offers a serious route to reducing avoidable nuclear costs and delays. More predictable regulation could help bring reliable low-carbon electricity and skilled employment. This is therefore a proposal whose potential benefits should be acknowledged. Its claimed immediacy still needs testing. The government's March 2026 response says it had accepted the principles of all 47 recommendations and begun implementation, with necessary legislation intended before the end of 2027, subject to parliamentary timings. Reform should identify which remaining actions it would accelerate and how, rather than presenting the whole programme as untouched. Changing guidance and legislation also requires trained regulators, competent project organisations and coordination across environmental and planning bodies. Even successful regulatory reform does not itself provide finance, construction teams or a completed reactor. The relevant test is a published delivery programme with responsibilities, milestones and safeguards. Consumers need an account of when electricity arrives and who carries construction risk, rather than a promise that an entire review can take effect at once.

articles.title: Automatically approve French and South Korean nuclear designs
articles.proposal: Legislate to recognise French and South Korean nuclear designs automatically as safe.
articles.counter: Using trusted overseas assessments can save time, but a design's nationality cannot establish its suitability for a particular British site and operator.
articles.critique: Reusing high-quality assessments from experienced overseas regulators could cut duplication and make established reactor designs easier to deploy. The benefit depends on the precise design version and evidence, rather than whether its vendor is French or South Korean. British nuclear approval separates generic design work from site licensing, environmental permits and planning decisions. Automatic recognition of a design would therefore leave practical questions about cooling, flooding, security, waste arrangements and the operator's capability. Those are matters for the actual project, not a foreign design certificate. ONR's May 2026 update already describes a policy for using international regulators' judgements, so the useful comparison is with that developing approach. Parliament would need to know what additional checks the proposal removes and what replaces them. Faster assessment is worthwhile where evidence supports it; removing independent judgement by nationality could instead create uncertainty over responsibility. Financing, supply chains and construction performance would remain essential even after design recognition.
